summary:
The Riau Islands stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is assessed as a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The source inventory records the same amended penal code as carrying up to one year in prison when a complaint is lodged, and the two figures are not reconciled here.

No province-specific divergence from that framework was found for the Riau Islands: private same-sex conduct is not criminalised in the province, but it attracts no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection either. Two other provinces of Indonesia, Aceh and South Sumatra, do criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions; in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. A 2020 raid case elsewhere in the country illustrates how enforcement varies with local regulation: those held were released because no regional regulation existed.

Physical risk is documented at national level. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and in July 2026 mobs attacked trans women in several provinces including West Java with no prosecutions reported; civil society describes conditions as rapidly worsening. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among non-military threats alongside terrorism and drug addiction, placing it inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion is sharply hostile and shapes the environment a visitor enters. Pew recorded 93% of Indonesians rating homosexuality morally unacceptable in 2025 and 95% opposition to same-sex marriage in 2023.

Indonesia has consistently opposed international scrutiny of these rules, voting against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025.

The provincial picture is uneven. Aceh and South Sumatra impose their own criminal provisions while the Riau Islands does not, so risk within Indonesia depends heavily on which province a visitor is standing in; Aceh's punishments under provincial religious law apply to anyone present there, including foreign visitors.

Reporting on Indonesia's trans community has focused on larger population centres, and the July 2026 attacks named West Java and other cities. No equivalent incident is documented for the Riau Islands in this inventory, which is an absence of reporting rather than evidence of safety.
localsOnly:
Residents of the Riau Islands live under the national penal code provision on extra-marital sex in force from 2 January 2026, with prosecutions reported as selective rather than systematic. Provincial religious criminal law of the Aceh type does not apply in this province.

Legal gender recognition for residents requires sex reassignment surgery followed by a judge's approval, and identity documents carry only 'male' or 'female' descriptors with no third-gender or X marker.

No national statute prohibits discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no hate-crime enhancement applies to violence against LGBT residents. There is likewise no statutory protection arising from the presidential decree of October 2025, which moves in the opposite direction by classifying the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture as a non-military threat.

Residents face the same expression offences as visitors: the 2006 pornography law reaches written and audio-visual material showing or suggesting same-sex relations with penalties up to seven years, and domestic online publishing of LGBT content exposes them to the blocked-platform environment and to the bill under discussion in 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty for the extra-marital sex provision is stated inconsistently across the sources: the national framework entry gives up to two years' imprisonment, while the amended penal code entry gives up to one year when a complaint is lodged. The discrepancy is unresolved in this inventory.

The inventory contains no unit-specific findings for the Riau Islands. Nothing is sourced on local police practice in the province, the content of provincial regulations (perda) on morality offences, documented violence against trans people here, or local facilities and healthcare access.

Entry and visa screening of trans visitors, including passport and marker checks at Riau Islands border posts, is not addressed by any source in this inventory and remains unresolved.

The relationship between the national decree of October 2025 and any provincial implementing measure in the Riau Islands is not sourced.
